title: Safe Handling of Workflow Expressions knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Safe Handling of Workflow Expressions?
options: Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
Do not interpolate untrusted event text directly into shell code; pass it through environment variables and quote and validate it as data.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
questions.answer_key: Do not interpolate untrusted event text directly into shell code; pass it through environment variables and quote and validate it as data.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of safe handling of workflow expressions: Do not interpolate untrusted event text directly into shell code; pass it through environment variables and quote and validate it as data. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to safe handling of workflow expressions?
options: Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: Do not interpolate untrusted event text directly into shell code; pass it through environment variables and quote and validate it as data. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
